A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same risk-sensitive diffusion framework. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization and retitling.

before.justification: v2 reports original synthetic experiments on stability and Gaussian/Cauchy corruption, plus evaluations on five real datasets in Appendix C, Figures 2–5, and Table 1.

after.justification: v3 retains these experiments and adds original MMD measurements, comparisons with additional methods, and noisy CIFAR-10 results in Appendix B, Tables 2–4.

M1.justification: The risk-sensitive VP/VE coefficients, instability objective, risk-free loss, training procedure, and zero-risk sampling are retained. v3's main-text algorithms summarize procedures also preserved in Appendix G; the image experiments do not establish a new method component.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic Gaussian mixtures, MIMIC-III, WARDS, Abalone, Telemonitoring, and Mushroom. v3 additionally evaluates image generation on CIFAR-10 with Gaussian pixel corruption, substantially extending the represented data domains beyond the earlier synthetic, tabular, and time-series coverage.

E2.justification: The original Table 1 comparator set is retained. v3 Table 3 newly evaluates Ambient Diffusion and Unbiased Diffusion Models against the proposed method on Abalone and Telemonitoring; these methods were only discussed in v2. Unbiased Diffusion Model also participates in the new CIFAR-10 comparison.

E3.justification: v3 adds MMD evaluation on two retained datasets and FID evaluation with 20% or 40% of CIFAR-10 images corrupted. It also changes the stated time-series risk input from Gaussian-process standard deviations in v2 Appendix C.2 to variances in v3 Section 5.2. This is a reported setting revision; unchanged Table 1 values do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Table 4 adds a limited robustness comparison across two fractions of corrupted training images, testing whether the method's advantage persists as corruption becomes more prevalent. The existing stability-interval demonstration, Gaussian-mixture bias analysis, and Cauchy-outlier study remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, performance confidence intervals, or significance tests for the model comparisons. Figure 1's retained 95% intervals describe Gaussian-process interpolation uncertainty, rather than uncertainty in comparative experimental results.

E6.justification: All 50 numerical entries in Table 1 are unchanged, as are the original plotted findings. New Tables 2–4 add substantial results: risk-sensitive VP SDE obtains MMD 0.00198 and 0.00717 on Abalone and Telemonitoring, and CIFAR-10 FID 4.89 and 6.97 at 20% and 40% corruption, versus 5.37 and 8.53 for Unbiased Diffusion Model. These are additional results, not improvements over v2 runs.

T1.justification: The central stability theorems, corollaries, and loss derivation are retained in Appendices E–G. Limited assumption changes include explicitly stating independence of the Gaussian noises in Lemma E.1's kernel proof and adding the T tending to infinity qualification to the prior-distribution discussion in Section 2.1.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a novel sample-risk setting, risk-sensitive diffusion, Gaussian perturbation stability, optimal mitigation of non-Gaussian perturbations, and improved generation from noisy data. v3 foregrounds non-image applications and empirical superiority, but the substantive central contributions remain the same.

C2.justification: v3 adds Remark 3.2 explaining corruption as generally irreversible local averaging and discusses alternative instability measures such as KL divergence as unexplored directions. Appendix B also interprets the image results as evidence of broader applicability. The existing Gaussian versus non-Gaussian stability limitations are retained.

D1.justification: v3 omits v2 Appendix C.2's WARDS implementation detail: a 0.01 probability of using the full time interval to accelerate convergence near zero. This removes reproducibility information without establishing that the heuristic was abandoned. v3 also promises code release upon acceptance, but supplies no code access.

R1.justification: v3 adds contextual references for non-image data, including Kaggle and van Breugel et al., and references for MMD, CIFAR-10, and KL divergence. Some general diffusion-background references are removed. The substantive positioning relative to Ambient Diffusion, Unbiased Diffusion Models, and conditional diffusion largely persists.

P1.justification: v3 extensively rewrites the abstract and introduction, adds explicit contributions and a conclusion, and reorganizes the paper around preliminaries, method, related work, and experiments. Detailed theory moves from main Sections 4–6 into Appendices E–G, while the earlier experimental appendix becomes main Section 5.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a conference layout, resizes and relocates Figures 2–5 and Table 1 into the main text, and revises captions. It adds Tables 2–4 and displays condensed training and sampling algorithms side by side while retaining fuller versions in Appendix G. The original plotted data are preserved.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses an empirical comparison gap by evaluating the previously discussed Ambient Diffusion and Unbiased Diffusion Models, while MMD and CIFAR-10 results provide additional corroboration. The reorganization also connects the method and evidence more clearly. These gains outweigh a limited reproducibility loss, but sparse new-experiment details, unchanged uncertainty reporting, the omitted WARDS heuristic, and the unexplained standard-deviation-to-variance revision limit the overall improvement.
